# Backtest: how good are simple, explainable demand forecasts?

*Generated by `scripts/backtest.py` from `data/demand_halfhourly.csv.gz`. Do not edit by hand. Per-group
numbers for both windows and every lead are in [`backtest_metrics.csv`](backtest_metrics.csv).*

Rolling-origin backtest of four baselines on every day from 2025-10-01 to 2026-09-30, in all 5 NEM regions,
1 to 7 days ahead. Times are NEM time (AEST); a half-hour belongs to the day it starts in.

## 1. Setup

**Target days:** every day from 2025-10-01 to 2026-09-30 (365 days, all four seasons), in all 5 regions.
**Origins:** midnight at the start of a day, knowing every half-hour before it and nothing after.
**Leads:** 1 to 7 days. Lead 1 is the *day-ahead* forecast; leads 1-7 pooled are the *week-ahead*
forecast (one forecast issued at midnight, scored over the whole week it covers). The target days are
the same at every lead, so leads compare like with like.

| Method | Forecast for a target day |
|---|---:|
| Naive (yesterday) | the last full day seen, repeated |
| Seasonal naive (last week) | the same weekday one week earlier |
| 4-week same-weekday mean | the average of the same weekday over the last 4 weeks |
| 3-year climatology | the same weekday within ±3 weeks of this date in each of the previous 3 years (21 days averaged) |

All four use only the same time of day, so the daily shape comes for free. The three weekly methods
also keep the day of the week; only the naive one ignores it. None of them use weather.

**Metrics** (all on half-hourly MW):
- **WAPE** = total absolute error / total absolute demand. The headline, because it stays meaningful
  when demand nears or crosses zero.
- **MAE** in MW, **bias** (mean forecast − actual; positive = over-forecast), and the mean error in
  each day's **peak** and **trough** (the daily max and min).
- **MAPE** is not used. South Australia shows why: its day-ahead MAPE ranges from
  704% to 1124% across the four methods, because a few half-hours with
  demand near zero dominate a mean of ratios, while its WAPE is 13.6%-18.7%.

## 2. Day-ahead: yesterday beats last week

Day-ahead WAPE (lower is better):

| Region | Naive | Seasonal naive | 4-week mean | Climatology | Best |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| NSW1 | 7.1% | 9.8% | 8.6% | 7.5% | Naive |
| QLD1 | 5.4% | 7.0% | 5.8% | 5.7% | Naive |
| VIC1 | 10.1% | 11.7% | 10.0% | 10.2% | 4-week mean |
| SA1 | 14.2% | 18.7% | 15.4% | 13.6% | Climatology |
| TAS1 | 6.4% | 7.8% | 6.8% | 10.9% | Naive |

The best day-ahead method in each region, in MW:

| Region | Best method | MAE | Daily peak error | Daily trough error | Bias |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| NSW1 | Naive | 525 | 588 | 596 | +0 |
| QLD1 | Naive | 332 | 302 | 496 | +0 |
| VIC1 | 4-week mean | 500 | 517 | 561 | -8 |
| SA1 | Climatology | 177 | 147 | 326 | -10 |
| TAS1 | Naive | 65 | 60 | 54 | +0 |

**Naive persistence (tomorrow = today) is the best day-ahead baseline in 3 of
5 regions** (NSW1, QLD1, TAS1); the others are 4-week mean in VIC1 (10.0%), climatology in SA1 (13.6%).
**Seasonal naive, the textbook baseline, comes last in 4 of 5.** Swapping last
week for yesterday cuts day-ahead error by 13%-28%.
The likeliest reason is weather: yesterday's is a far better guide to tomorrow's than last week's,
and over one day that matters more than getting the day of the week right. Section 5 shows the cost of ignoring the
weekday, which is where naive loses.

## 3. Week-ahead: averages beat persistence

Week-ahead WAPE (a forecast issued at midnight, scored over all 7 days it covers):

| Region | Naive | Seasonal naive | 4-week mean | Climatology | Best |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| NSW1 | 9.9% | 9.8% | 8.6% | 7.5% | Climatology |
| QLD1 | 7.4% | 7.0% | 5.8% | 5.7% | Climatology |
| VIC1 | 12.7% | 11.7% | 10.0% | 10.2% | 4-week mean |
| SA1 | 18.5% | 18.7% | 15.4% | 13.6% | Climatology |
| TAS1 | 7.7% | 7.8% | 6.8% | 10.9% | 4-week mean |

Naive WAPE by lead (days ahead). The other three methods look back whole weeks, so for leads 1-7
they use exactly the same days and their error is the same at every lead:

| Region | Lead 1 | Lead 2 | Lead 3 | Lead 4 | Lead 5 | Lead 6 | Lead 7 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| NSW1 | 7.1% | 9.6% | 10.6% | 11.1% | 11.0% | 10.3% | 9.8% |
| QLD1 | 5.4% | 7.4% | 8.0% | 8.3% | 8.4% | 7.6% | 7.0% |
| VIC1 | 10.1% | 13.1% | 13.9% | 14.1% | 13.8% | 12.5% | 11.7% |
| SA1 | 14.2% | 18.6% | 19.8% | 20.0% | 19.8% | 18.6% | 18.7% |
| TAS1 | 6.4% | 7.6% | 7.7% | 8.1% | 8.4% | 8.0% | 7.8% |

Persistence decays fast. From lead 2 on, naive is not the best method in any
region; its error peaks at lead
4-5, and recovers at lead 7, where "the last day seen" is the same weekday
and naive becomes seasonal naive. Over a whole week, **the 3-year climatology is the best baseline in
3 of 5 regions** (NSW1, QLD1, SA1), and the 4-week mean in the rest
(VIC1, TAS1). Averaging many similar days washes out
one-off weather, which a single copied day can't do.

![Error by lead time](charts/backtest_error_by_lead.png)

## 4. Where in the day the error sits: midday

Share of each region's day-ahead absolute error (best method) that falls between 10:00 and 16:00,
a quarter of the day, and how much larger the average midday error is than at other times:

| Region | Best day-ahead method | Error share 10:00-16:00 | Midday vs rest of day |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| NSW1 | Naive | 42% | 2.2× |
| QLD1 | Naive | 43% | 2.3× |
| VIC1 | 4-week mean | 40% | 2.0× |
| SA1 | Climatology | 49% | 2.8× |
| TAS1 | Naive | 29% | 1.2× |

On the mainland, 40%-49% of the
error lands in the 25% of the day between 10:00 and 16:00, where midday half-hours miss by
2.0-2.8× as much as the rest. That fits
rooftop solar: cloud cover decides how much demand the grid sees at noon, and none of these
baselines know tomorrow's cloud. The two ends agree. SA1, where weekday midday demand is only
66% of the all-day average this year (the deepest solar dip), has the most midday-heavy
error (2.8×); TAS1, at 94% (the shallowest dip), has the flattest
(1.2×).

![Day-ahead error by time of day](charts/backtest_error_by_time_of_day.png)

## 5. Which days break the baselines

Day-ahead WAPE by day of the week (target day), naive vs seasonal naive:

| Region / method | Mon | Tue | Wed | Thu | Fri | Sat | Sun |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| NSW1 naive | 9.4% | 6.6% | 5.7% | 6.2% | 5.3% | 8.7% | 7.7% |
| NSW1 seasonal naive | 9.2% | 8.9% | 9.0% | 9.4% | 10.2% | 11.9% | 10.4% |
| QLD1 naive | 7.8% | 5.1% | 4.2% | 3.8% | 4.8% | 7.2% | 4.6% |
| QLD1 seasonal naive | 7.8% | 8.0% | 6.6% | 6.6% | 6.4% | 6.9% | 6.4% |
| VIC1 naive | 13.5% | 8.9% | 9.0% | 8.3% | 7.9% | 13.2% | 10.1% |
| VIC1 seasonal naive | 11.6% | 11.6% | 10.8% | 11.8% | 12.7% | 12.2% | 10.9% |
| SA1 naive | 16.2% | 13.1% | 12.5% | 12.0% | 12.4% | 17.4% | 16.3% |
| SA1 seasonal naive | 19.0% | 18.9% | 19.0% | 19.3% | 18.0% | 18.6% | 18.0% |
| TAS1 naive | 7.3% | 6.6% | 5.9% | 6.5% | 5.6% | 7.1% | 5.8% |
| TAS1 seasonal naive | 8.2% | 8.0% | 8.5% | 7.9% | 6.8% | 6.7% | 8.2% |

**Naive fails on the days the week changes shape.** Its Monday and Saturday error is
1.2-1.7× its Tuesday-Friday error, because Monday
is forecast from a Sunday and Saturday from a Friday. Seasonal naive doesn't have that problem, but it
pays for it every other day.

**Holidays are the hardest days.** The 10 days from 24 Dec to 2 Jan are 3% of the
year but carry 4%-7% of seasonal naive's day-ahead error,
1.3-2.6× their share, because each holiday is forecast from an ordinary day a week
earlier. Christmas Day is among the three worst days for the best method in
**4 of 5 regions** (NSW1, QLD1, VIC1, SA1).

The three worst day-ahead days for each region's best method (that day's WAPE):

| Region | Method | Worst | 2nd | 3rd |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| NSW1 | Naive | Thu 25 Dec 2025 (26%) | Sun 07 Dec 2025 (25%) | Sun 11 Jan 2026 (24%) |
| QLD1 | Naive | Sat 28 Mar 2026 (19%) | Sat 14 Mar 2026 (17%) | Thu 25 Dec 2025 (16%) |
| VIC1 | 4-week mean | Thu 25 Dec 2025 (49%) | Fri 26 Dec 2025 (48%) | Thu 01 Jan 2026 (38%) |
| SA1 | Climatology | Mon 09 Mar 2026 (54%) | Wed 04 Mar 2026 (51%) | Thu 25 Dec 2025 (47%) |
| TAS1 | Naive | Mon 03 Nov 2025 (17%) | Sun 02 Nov 2025 (16%) | Sat 08 Nov 2025 (16%) |

## 6. Does the ranking hold? The year before

The same backtest on the previous 12 months (2024-10-01 to 2025-09-30):

| Horizon | Region | Best, latest year | WAPE | Best, year before | WAPE |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Day-ahead | NSW1 | Naive | 7.1% | Naive | 7.3% |
| Day-ahead | QLD1 | Naive | 5.4% | Naive | 5.3% |
| Day-ahead | VIC1 | 4-week mean | 10.0% | Climatology | 10.8% |
| Day-ahead | SA1 | Climatology | 13.6% | Naive | 13.5% |
| Day-ahead | TAS1 | Naive | 6.4% | Naive | 5.7% |
| Week-ahead | NSW1 | Climatology | 7.5% | Climatology | 7.7% |
| Week-ahead | QLD1 | Climatology | 5.7% | Climatology | 6.1% |
| Week-ahead | VIC1 | 4-week mean | 10.0% | Climatology | 10.8% |
| Week-ahead | SA1 | Climatology | 13.6% | Climatology | 14.1% |
| Week-ahead | TAS1 | 4-week mean | 6.8% | 4-week mean | 6.0% |

The best method is the same in **7 of 10** region-horizon pairs. Climatology is the one
to watch: it averages the three previous years, so a shift in a region's level shows up as bias. In
the latest year its bias was NSW1 +52 MW (+0.7%), QLD1 -71 MW (-1.2%), VIC1 -258 MW (-5.1%), SA1 -10 MW (-0.8%), TAS1 +104 MW (+10.2%)
of average demand, largest relative to its size in TAS1. Regions where climatology's day-ahead WAPE got worse
by more than one point year on year: TAS1 (+2.3 points). A long-run average is only as good as the
assumption that the level hasn't moved.

## 7. The bar for Part 3

The best baseline per region and horizon (latest year). A method in Part 3 is only worth its extra
complexity if it beats these:

| Region | Day-ahead (WAPE) | Week-ahead (WAPE) | Day-ahead MAE |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| New South Wales | Naive, 7.1% | Climatology, 7.5% | 525 MW |
| Queensland | Naive, 5.4% | Climatology, 5.7% | 332 MW |
| Victoria | 4-week mean, 10.0% | 4-week mean, 10.0% | 500 MW |
| South Australia | Climatology, 13.6% | Climatology, 13.6% | 177 MW |
| Tasmania | Naive, 6.4% | 4-week mean, 6.8% | 65 MW |

## What this means for operations planning

- **Pick the baseline by horizon.** For tomorrow, copy today (3 of 5
  regions); for next week, average many similar days. The textbook seasonal naive is the wrong default
  at both horizons here.
- **The hard part is the middle of the day.** 40%-49%
  of mainland day-ahead error sits between 10:00 and 16:00. Buffers and battery plans should be
  sized for the midday trough, not only the evening peak, and the method that most improves on these
  baselines will be the one that knows about tomorrow's cloud and temperature (Part 3).
- **Calendar effects are cheap to fix.** Naive's Monday and Saturday error runs
  1.2-1.7× its midweek error, and Christmas Day is among the
  three worst days in 4 of 5 regions. A day-type rule (yesterday on ordinary
  weekdays, last week after the weekend changes shape, a holiday calendar) costs nothing in
  explainability.
- **Watch the level.** A long-run average carries a level shift straight into the forecast as bias,
  so it needs a recent-level correction before it can be trusted on its own.
